title: Advising parents about a music career and money
summary: She tells parents jazz is not for those wanting money; Broadway doubling is the best-paid steady work, but family life needs a spouse with a stable career.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: And when Mom and Dad come to you and say what do you think about my son or daughter making a career in music, do you have a — what do you tell them?

Well so far, I mean I don’t think any of these people are really thinking that at this point. I think they look at it like with sports — like something that’s going to help them get into college. Or I don’t know. But I mean if they said it or if they do occasionally say it to me, or if the kid says it, then I try to just explain to them, you know, that it’s not easy and if they want a lot of money they shouldn’t do it.
Right. That’s a bit of an oxymoron — I’m going to go into jazz to make money.
Yeah. I mean if you’re a person who needs a lot of money to live comfortably than you should not, I think, be a jazz musician. And that if they do want to make a lot of money
as a musician basically the way that I know to do it is to play a Broadway show. So you have to be a good doubler.
They make, I think, a ton and then it’s fairly stable. Or maybe not so much now but I mean some shows close and some are cutting down on their orchestras.
Yeah. It’s almost like having a nine to five except it’s more like a, whatever, seven to ten.

It is. And playing the same thing every night couldn’t be too much fun but yeah, if you’re a person who wants to marry, have kids, have a house, have a car, then you can’t fit being a jazz musician into that unless the person you marry has a stable career. I would tell them things like that. Yeah, I mean it’s clear.
